CERVICAL CANCER
Group 3A/18A
Sophia Benson, Kristeen Brown, Carina Buslovich, 
Sabrina Madani, Jaime Saulle, Varuna Shekar, 
Olivia Tymon
Fall 2026 | Medical Surgical III | Dr. Coccimiglio

RISK F ACTORS/ PREVENTION/ HEAL TH PROMOTION/ EARL Y 
DETECTION 
Risk Factors: 
• HPV 16 and 18 -> Over 99% of cases 
• Other STIs 
• Chronic cervical infections 
• Family history 
• Prolonged oral contraceptive use (>5 
years) 
• Multiple sexual partners or a partner 
who has had many sexual partners 
• 3 or more births and young age of 
first birth 
• Exposure to diethylstilbestro in utero 
• Smoking 
 
Prevention and Health Promotion: 
• Two dose series of HPV vaccine beginning 
at age 9 
• Safe sexual practices 
• Smoking cessation 
• Routine and early screening 
Early Detection: 
• Pap smears! (cervical cytology) 
• ACOG recommends every 3 years starting 
from age 21 
• Begin high risk HPV testing from ages 31-
65 
• Routine screening and sexual health 
appointments

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS
 
Early cervical cancer may be asymptomatic, making routine screening important.  
• Abnormal vaginal bleeding  
⚬ Bleeding after sexual intercourse (postcoital bleeding)  
⚬ Bleeding between menstrual periods  
⚬ Heavier or longer menstrual periods 
• Abnormal vaginal discharge  
⚬ Watery, bloody, or foul-smelling discharge  
• Pelvic symptoms  
⚬ Pelvic or lower abdominal pain  
⚬ Pain during sexual intercourse (dyspareunia)  
• Advanced disease  
⚬ Difficulty or pain with urination  
⚬ Blood in the urine or stool  
⚬ Leg swelling  
⚬ Back or flank pain  
⚬ Weight loss, fatigue, or decreased appetite 
Nursing Focus: Recognize abnormal bleeding/discharge and persistent pelvic symptoms and encourage 
prompt evaluation and follow-up.

MEDICAL MANAGEMENT
There are many different ways to manage cervical cancer, and treatment really depends on the individual patient. Everyone’s situation is a 
little different, so their care should be personalized to what they need and feel comfortable with. It’s also important to consider their 
cultural beliefs, personal choices, and autonomy. At the end of the day, the patient and healthcare team should work together to find a 
treatment plan that feels right for that specific patient and supports them throughout their care. 
Surgical Treatment
• Hysterectomy: removes the body of the uterus and the cervix, laparoscopically or through a surgical incision
• Trachelectomy: removes the cervix and the upper part of the vagina, but not the uterus. This option preserves the patient’s ability to bear children
• Lymph Node Dissection: removal of the lymph nodes surrounding the cervix to prevent metastasis
Chemotherapy
• Slows the growth and destroys cancer cells from the body
• Common chemo medications include cisplatin, carboplatin, or paclitaxel
• Can be given in combination with radiation to increase its effectiveness
Targeted therapy
• T argets specific proteins or pathways that cancer cells use to grow
• Bevacizumab or Pembrolizumab may be used for certain advanced or recurrent cancers
Immunotherapy
• Assists the immune system by recognizing the cancer cells and destroying their growth 
• Can also be combined with chemotherapy and/or targeted therapy depending on the cancer manifestations
Palliative treatment
• Unfortunately, in advanced cancers/stages, palliative treatment may the only treatment option
• Behavioral therapy, pain management, and “bucket list” experiences can help the patient accept the prognosis and enjoy their end of life stage

Drug Use Nursing Responsibilities
Chemotherapy 
Agents
Cisplatin Platinum agent given with radiation, radiosensitizer
Provide IV hydation before and after chemotherapy sessions. Monitor 
creatinine, I&O, serum electrolytes, assess hearing.
Carboplatin Cisplatin alternative with lower systemic toxicity Monitor for low thrombocytopenia. Implement bleeding precautions. 
Paclitaxel
Advanced/recurrent cancer, used in combination 
with cisplatin
Administer premedication regimen to prevent acute hypersensitivity.  
Assess for allergic reaction. Monitor for neuropathy. 
Targeted 
Therapy
Bevacizumab
Used in combination with chemotherapy agents to 
cut off blood supply of tumor
Report signs of hypertension to the provider. Monitor for bleeding or 
excessive fatigue. Hold medication before and after surgery to prevent 
delayed wound healing.
Immunotherapy Pembrolizumab
Helps the immune system recognize cancerous 
cells
Assess and document baseline organ function. Monitor for signs of 
immune-mediated adverse reactions. 
MEDICATION MANAGEMENT AND NURSING RESPONSIBILITIES
Supportive medications include; antiemetics to give prior to chemotherapy sessions, growth factor medications to increase the production 
of neutrophils and prevent anemia and analgesics for pain.
Core Nursing Responsibilities
• Prior to chemotherapy cycles, establish baseline labs of CBC, renal and liver function, and electrolytes.
⚬ Hold chemotherapy procedures and notify the provider if lab values or vital signs suggest low blood counts, active infection, decreased 
liver or kidney function
• Educate the patient on utilizing contraception during and after treatments, reporting a fever or bleeding, and maintaining adequate 
hydration
• Ensure appropriate PPE is worn at all times when handling chemotherapy supplies and continue with body-fluid precautions until told 
by the provider

P ATIENT AND F AMIL Y EDUCATION
• Fatigue, skin and cervical tissue changes from external and internal radiation, nausea, and hair loss from 
chemotherapy can occur. Mild unscented soap should be used on radiation sites, and the skin should be pat dry. 
Loose cotton clothing and underwear should be worn to minimize irritation. A fever over 100.4°F, severe abdominal 
pain, heavy vaginal bleeding, or foul-smelling discharge should be reported to the provider.
• Pelvic and vaginal discomfort can impact intercourse. Vaginal dilators may be prescribed after radiation to prevent 
stenosis. The dilator is inserted into the vagina with a water-based lubricant and kept in place for 10-15 minutes, 2-4 
times per week.
• Local cervical cancer support groups can be found on the National Cervical Cancer Coalition website, nccc-
online.org.
DISCHARGE PLANNING AND HOMECARE
• Medication reconciliation should be completed prior to discharge. All medications should be reviewed with the 
patient. 
• If the patient had a pelvic exenteration or hysterectomy, proper wound care should be demonstrated using the 
teach-back method. Foley catheter care instructions may also be required if not removed before discharge. 
• Patients should avoid heavy lifting and strenuous exercise. Pelvic insertion (i.e. tampons, intercourse) should be 
avoided until clearance from the provider. 
• Patients may be referred for CHHA services including RN, P/T, or O/T visits to monitor wound healing and prevent 
post-op deconditioning.

NCLEX STYLE QUESTION #1
A community health nurse is developing an educational PowerPoint for a 
seminar focused on reducing the incidence of cervical cancer. Which 
primary prevention strategy should the nurse emphasize? 
 
A. Undergoing annual Pap Smear screenings starting at 21 
B. Receiving the recombinant HPV vaccination series 
C. Scheduling routine biannual colposcopic evaluations  
D. Initiating high-sensitivity serum tumor marker testing annually

ANSWER + RATIONALE 
A: INCORRECT; PAP SMEARS ARE A FORM OF SECONDARY PREVENTION BECAUSE 
THEY CAN DETECT PRE-EXISTING CELLULAR CHANGES RATHER THAN PREVENTING THE 
DISEASE FORM OCCURRING 
B: CORRECT; PRIMARY PREVENTION PURPOSES IS TO PREVENT A DISEASE BEFORE IT 
OCCURS. HPV VACCINE PREVENTS INFECTION BY THE VIRAL STRAINS RESPONSIBLE 
FOR MANY CERVICAL CANCERS  
C: INCORRECT; A COLPOSCOPY IS DONE AS A FOLLOW UP DIAGNOSTIC PROCEDURE 
AFTER AN ABNORMAL SCREENING RESULT IS FOUND. THIS IS A SECONDARY 
PREVENTION METHOD  
D: INCORRECT; SERUM TUMOR MARKER TESTING IS NORMALLY DONE TO MONITOR 
RESPONSE TO A TREATMENT OR TO DETECT A REOCCURRENCE IN PATIENTS WHO 
HAVE ALREADY BEEN DIAGNOSED WITH CERVICAL CANCER

NCLEX STYLE QUESTION #2
A nurse is providing discharge instructions to a client who underwent a 
radical hysterectomy for early-stage cervical cancer. Which of the 
following client statements indicates a correct understanding of home care 
restrictions?
A. “I am able to resume my high-impact exercise regimen as soon as I am 
home”
B. “ I can relax and take a hot bubble bath the same night I get home”
C. “I should avoid lifting any objects heavier than 10lbs”
D. “I am allowed to engage in sexual intercourse since my incision is 
closed with staples”

ANSWER + RATIONALE 
 A. INCORRECT; ALL STRENUOUS ACTIVITIES AND EXCERSICE SHOULD BE STRICLY 
AVOIDED DURING THE INITIAL RECOVERY PERIOD  
B. INCORRECT; TUB BATHS ARE PROHIBITED UNTIL CLEARED BY THE PROVIDER BECAUSE 
WATER CAN INTRODUCE BACTERIA INTO THE SITE, SIGNIFICANTLY INCREASING THE RISK 
OF PELVIC INFECTION.
C. CORRECT; PATIENTS MUST AVOID LIFTING OBJECTS HEAVIER THAN 10 POUNDS FOR 
ATLEAST 6 WEEKS FOLLOWING PELVIC SURGERY TO ALLOW PROPER HEALING OF THE 
INTERNAL VAGINAL CUFF AND ABDOMINAL WALL
D. INCORRECT;ALTHOUGH THE SKIN INCISION HEALS QUICKLY, THE INTERNAL MUSCLES 
REQUIRE SEVERAL WEEKS TO HEAL FULLY. SEXUAL INTERCOURSE IS STRICTLY 
CONTRAINDICATED FOR 6 WEEKS POSTOPERATIVELY TO PREVENT VAGINAL CUFF 
DEHISCENCE AND HEMORRHAGE.
